title: kids · children · young people · juveniles · minors
takeaway: Same people, different lens: family life (kids), neutral (children), policy (young people), law (juveniles, minors).

words.note: Everyday speech. Fine in informal writing, avoid in reports.
words.example: Are the kids coming to the barbecue?

words.note: Default word. Suggests younger ages (roughly under 13).
words.example: The museum is free for children under 12.

words.note: Policy, education, NGOs. Usually teenagers and young adults.
words.example: The scheme aims to help young people into work.

words.note: Legal/police context. Can sound cold or stigmatising elsewhere.
words.example: Two juveniles were detained after the incident.

words.note: Legal status (under the age of majority): consent, alcohol, contracts.
words.example: Alcohol may not be sold to minors.

drills.prompt: A text to your sister: “Want me to pick up the ___ from school?”
Government report: “Unemployment among ___ aged 16–24 has risen.”
Website terms: “This service is not available to ___.”

title: get · obtain · acquire · procure · gain
takeaway: “Get” is never wrong in speech. In writing, choose by HOW the thing is obtained: effort (procure), over time (acquire, gain), formally (obtain).

words.note: All-purpose. Overused in essays: replace it there.
words.example: Did you get the tickets?

words.note: Formal equivalent of get, especially documents, data, permission.
words.example: Participants' consent was obtained before the interviews.

words.note: Gradually (skills, knowledge, a taste) or by purchase (companies).
words.example: Google acquired the startup for $2 billion.

words.note: Obtain with effort, often official purchasing (procurement). Can imply something shady in some contexts.
words.example: The ministry struggled to procure enough vaccines.

words.note: Get something valuable through effort or over time.
words.example: I gained a lot of experience during my apprenticeship.

drills.prompt: CV: “___ hands-on experience with React and PostgreSQL.”
Methodology: “Data were ___ from the national statistics office.”
“The firm was ___ by a larger competitor in 2021.”

title: big · large · considerable · substantial · significant
takeaway: Big and large are about physical size. For abstract amounts and effects in writing: considerable, substantial, significant (careful: in science, “significant” means statistically significant).

words.note: Speech. Also emotional importance (a big decision).
words.example: That's a big mistake.

words.note: Physical size, numbers, quantities. Not for emotions (not “a large mistake”).
words.example: A large number of students applied.

words.note: Large enough to matter; often effort, time, money, interest.
words.example: The project required considerable effort.

words.note: Large and solid, real. Amounts, evidence, changes.
words.example: There is substantial evidence for this claim.

words.note: Important/noticeable. In research papers, it implies statistical significance.
words.example: The policy had a significant impact on enrolment.

drills.prompt: Casual: “Getting that job was a ___ deal for me.”
Formal: “The renovation was carried out at ___ cost.”
Research: “There is ___ evidence that sleep affects memory.”
drills.why: Evidence that is solid and plentiful.

title: say · claim · argue · maintain · assert · suggest
takeaway: Reporting verbs reveal YOUR stance: claim distances you, argue presents reasoning, suggest is tentative, maintain implies persistence despite opposition.

words.note: Neutral, no stance.
words.example: The report says that costs rose.

words.note: Suggests the writer isn't sure it's true.
words.example: The company claims its app is 100% secure.

words.note: Presents a position supported by reasoning.
words.example: Smith argues that remote work boosts productivity.

words.note: Keeps saying it, often despite doubts or criticism.
words.example: He maintains that he was never informed.

words.note: States confidently and forcefully.
words.example: The author asserts that the policy has failed.

words.note: Tentative, especially for evidence (the data suggest…).
words.example: The results suggest a link between the two.

drills.prompt: You doubt it: “The influencer ___ that the supplement cures anxiety.”
Cautious evidence: “These figures ___ that demand is slowing.”
Despite the evidence, the suspect ___ his innocence.

title: problem · issue · challenge · concern · setback
takeaway: Professional English softens problems: issue (neutral), challenge (positive spin), concern (worry), setback (temporary). Overusing “challenge” sounds like corporate spin.

words.note: Direct. Fine, but can sound alarming to clients.
words.example: We have a problem with the server.

words.note: The standard professional word. Also: topic of debate.
words.example: We're aware of the issue and working on a fix.

words.note: Difficulty framed as something to overcome.
words.example: Scaling the team will be our main challenge this year.

words.note: A worry. Raise concerns = express worry formally.
words.example: Several students raised concerns about the new grading system.

words.note: Something that delays progress, usually temporary.
words.example: Losing our lead developer was a serious setback.

drills.prompt: Status page: “We're investigating an ___ affecting payments.”
Staff meeting: “Several employees have raised ___ about the new policy.”
“The failed test was a ___, but we're still on track for launch.”

title: help · assist · aid · support · facilitate
takeaway: “Help” is the default. Assist = formal help (often a secondary role). Facilitate = make a process easier, not help a person.

words.note: Default, everywhere.
words.example: Can you help me fix this bug?

words.note: Formal; often suggests a supporting role. NOT “assister à”.
words.example: Our staff will be happy to assist you.

words.note: Formal/technical; also humanitarian aid (noun).
words.example: Diagrams aid understanding.

words.note: Ongoing help or encouragement; backing an idea.
words.example: My manager fully supported my training plan.

words.note: Make a process easier. Takes a thing as object, not a person.
words.example: The new tool facilitates collaboration across teams.

drills.prompt: Formal notice: “Staff are available to ___ passengers with reduced mobility.”
“Shared documentation ___ knowledge transfer between teams.”
Friend: “Can you ___ me move on Saturday?”

title: start · begin · commence · launch · initiate
takeaway: Start/begin are interchangeable in most cases. Commence is formal and sounds pompous in speech. Launch = start something new publicly. Initiate = set a process in motion.

words.note: Default. Also for machines (start the car).
words.example: Let's start with a quick recap.

words.note: Slightly more formal/literary than start.
words.example: I began to realise the project was too ambitious.

words.note: Official announcements, legal texts. Odd in conversation.
words.example: Construction will commence in March.

words.note: Start something new and public: product, campaign, investigation.
words.example: We're launching the beta next week.

words.note: Set a process in motion; also technical (initiate a connection).
words.example: The client initiates the TLS handshake.

drills.prompt: Casual meeting: “OK, shall we get ___?”
drills.why: “Get started” is the natural spoken form.

drills.prompt: Press release: “The company will ___ its new app in June.”
Networking: “The client ___ the connection with a SYN packet.”
drills.why: Technical: sets a process in motion.

title: show · demonstrate · illustrate · indicate · reveal
takeaway: Choose by strength of evidence: demonstrate (proves) > show > indicate (points to) > suggest. Illustrate = give an example. Reveal = uncover something hidden.

words.note: Default.
words.example: The graph shows a steady rise.

words.note: Prove clearly; also to show how something works.
words.example: The experiment demonstrates that the effect is real.

words.note: Explain through an example.
words.example: This case illustrates the risks of poor security.

words.note: Point towards; weaker than show.
words.example: Early data indicate a slight improvement.

words.note: Make known something previously hidden or unknown.
words.example: The audit revealed several vulnerabilities.

drills.prompt: Weak evidence: “Preliminary results ___ a possible link.”
Example: “The Equifax breach ___ how costly a single unpatched server can be.”
drills.why: An example of a general point.

drills.prompt: Hidden info: “The investigation ___ that data had been sold.”
